stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 8 hours after swallowing about 30 g of acetaminophen tablets. He has had nausea and has vomited twice, but he is alert and breathing normally. Examination is otherwise normal. His serum acetaminophen concentration plots in the toxic range on the treatment nomogram and aminotransferases are normal.
oneliner: 17M + 30 g acetaminophen 8 hours ago + nausea and vomiting + alert, breathing normally + toxic nomogram level + normal aminotransferases → best treatment?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

whyNot.A: Blocks alcohol dehydrogenase for **methanol or ethylene glycol**; his ingestion was **acetaminophen**
whyNot.B: Reverses opioids; he is **alert and breathing normally**, and the ingestion was **acetaminophen**
whyNot.D: Used for **salicylate or tricyclic** poisoning; his ingestion was **acetaminophen alone**

why: A **toxic acetaminophen level at 8 hours** is treated with N-acetylcysteine. It **restores hepatic glutathione** so the toxic metabolite NAPQI is neutralized. Treatment started **within 8 hours** gives almost complete protection from liver injury.

idea.rule: Match the antidote to the toxin.
also: Methanol or ethylene glycol: fomepizole
Opioids: naloxone
Iron: deferoxamine
Organophosphates: atropine and pralidoxime

stem: A new antihypertensive that has passed animal studies is given for the first time in humans to 20 healthy volunteers. Investigators measure the half-life, how well it is tolerated and its side effects across a range of doses.
oneliner: New drug first in humans, 20 healthy volunteers + half-life and side effects measured → which phase?
ask: Which stage of drug development is this?

whyNot.A: Preclinical work is in **cells and animals**; here humans already receive the drug
whyNot.C: Phase 2 tests **efficacy and dosing in patients** with the disease; these are healthy volunteers
whyNot.D: Phase 3 compares against standard therapy in **large patient groups**, not 20 volunteers
whyNot.E: Phase 4 is **post-marketing surveillance** after approval; the drug is new

why: Phase 1 gives a new drug to a **small number of healthy volunteers** to test **safety and pharmacokinetics**. Phase 2 tests efficacy and dosing in a small group of patients; phase 3 compares it with standard treatment in large groups.

idea.rule: Phase 1 = safety and PK in healthy volunteers; phase 2 = efficacy in a few patients; phase 3 = large comparison; phase 4 = post-marketing.
also: Phase 4 detects rare adverse effects
Phase 3 data support FDA approval
Cancer phase 1 trials often enroll patients
Phase 2 gives the first efficacy data

stem: A 34-year-old woman who lives in a basement apartment has had headache, nausea and dizziness for two weeks, beginning when the weather turned cold. Her husband and two children have similar complaints, and all feel better after a day away from home. Her vital signs and examination are normal.
oneliner: 34F + basement flat + winter headache, nausea, dizziness + whole household affected, better away from home → which history question next?
ask: Which of the following history questions is most helpful next?

options.A: Recent travel abroad by anyone in the household
options.B: Daily use of over-the-counter pain medication
options.C: The type of heating system used in the home
options.D: A family history of recurrent migraine headaches
options.E: Recent sick contacts at her place of work

whyNot.A: Travel brings infections or malaria, but it would not explain a **whole household improving when away from home**
whyNot.B: Analgesic-overuse headache affects **one person**, not four, and does not track the season or the place
whyNot.D: Migraine runs in families but does not cause **simultaneous symptoms in everyone** sharing the home
whyNot.E: Sick contacts at work would not affect the **family, who share the home but not her workplace**

answer: Source of home heating (carbon monoxide exposure)
why: **Several household members** with headache and nausea that **ease away from home in winter** point to **carbon monoxide** from a faulty or unvented heater. CO binds hemoglobin, shifts the curve left and blocks tissue oxygen delivery; treat with **100% oxygen**.

idea.rule: A cluster of vague symptoms in one household in cold weather = carbon monoxide until proven otherwise.
also: Cherry-red skin is a late and unreliable sign
Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal
Treat with 100% oxygen or hyperbaric oxygen
Delayed neurologic sequelae can follow severe exposure

stem: A 41-year-old man with schizophrenia was started on haloperidol 4 days ago. He is now confused and sweating heavily, with a temperature of 40.1 C, a heart rate that swings between 90 and 140/min, labile blood pressure and marked stiffness of all limbs. Reflexes are normal with no clonus. Creatine kinase is 9,800 U/L.
oneliner: 41M + haloperidol started 4 days ago + fever 40.1 + lead-pipe rigidity, no clonus + labile vitals + sweating + CK 9,800 → treatment?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Stop haloperidol, start cooling and give dantrolene
options.B: Give cyproheptadine and carry on with the haloperidol
options.C: Add benztropine alone and keep the haloperidol dose
options.D: Give physostigmine to reverse the anticholinergic state
options.E: Raise the haloperidol dose to settle the agitation

whyNot.B: Cyproheptadine treats **serotonin syndrome**, but he has **no clonus**, and the **offending antipsychotic would stay on**
whyNot.C: Benztropine treats simple **parkinsonism**; with fever and CK in the thousands the **culprit drug must stop**
whyNot.D: Physostigmine reverses **anticholinergic toxicity** (dry, hot skin); this man is **sweating heavily** and rigid
whyNot.E: More D2 blockade **worsens neuroleptic malignant syndrome**

answer: Stop the antipsychotic, cool and support, give dantrolene (or bromocriptine)
why: **High-potency antipsychotic**, **lead-pipe rigidity**, **hyperthermia**, autonomic instability and **high CK** make neuroleptic malignant syndrome. First **stop the antipsychotic**, then cooling, fluids and **dantrolene or bromocriptine**.

idea.rule: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: remove the dopamine blocker, then cool and relax muscle.
also: Dantrolene blocks ryanodine receptor calcium release
Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist that restores D2 tone
Fluids protect the kidneys from rhabdomyolysis
Dantrolene also treats malignant hyperthermia

stem: A 38-year-old man drank an unlabeled windshield-washer fluid 6 hours ago. After a fomepizole dose, he still has bicarbonate of 8 mEq/L, pH 7.08 and cannot see more than shadows. Methanol level is markedly raised.
oneliner: 38M + methanol ingestion + bicarbonate 8 and pH 7.08 + visual loss despite fomepizole → additional treatment?
ask: Which of the following additional treatments is most appropriate?

options.A: N-acetylcysteine given as a loading and maintenance infusion
options.B: Hemodialysis, with folate to speed formate clearance
options.C: Deferoxamine given as a continuous intravenous infusion
options.D: Sodium thiosulfate given with sodium nitrite
options.E: Pralidoxime given with atropine to treat the poisoning

whyNot.A: N-acetylcysteine is the antidote for **acetaminophen**, which does not cause visual loss with acidosis
whyNot.C: Deferoxamine chelates **iron**, and this man has no iron ingestion
whyNot.D: Thiosulfate is for **cyanide**; **formate, not cyanide**, is the toxin
whyNot.E: Pralidoxime is for **organophosphates**, with miosis and secretions

why: **Severe acidosis** and **visual symptoms** after methanol mean the toxic metabolite is already formed, so add **hemodialysis** to remove methanol and formate. **Folate** helps liver enzymes convert formate to CO2; fomepizole only blocks further production.

idea.rule: Fomepizole stops new toxic metabolite, but dialysis removes what is already there.
also: Dialysis also treats severe ethylene glycol poisoning
Dialysis treats severe salicylate toxicity
Dialysis treats severe lithium toxicity
Dialysis treats severe metformin-associated lactic acidosis

stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought in after swallowing several of her mother's prenatal vitamin tablets. She has vomited several times, has bloody diarrhea, and is lethargic. Blood gas shows metabolic acidosis, and an abdominal x-ray shows radiopaque pills in the stomach.
oneliner: 2F + swallowed mother's vitamin tablets + vomiting + bloody diarrhea + metabolic acidosis + radiopaque pills → antidote?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate antidote?

whyNot.A: Succimer is an oral chelator for **mild lead** poisoning, not iron
whyNot.B: Dimercaprol is used with **lead, arsenic or mercury**, not iron
whyNot.C: Penicillamine treats **Wilson disease** (copper) and lead, not acute iron overdose

why: **Prenatal vitamins (iron)**, **vomiting and bloody diarrhea**, **metabolic acidosis** and **radiopaque pills** point to acute iron toxicity. **Deferoxamine** chelates free iron and is the antidote.

idea.rule: Iron overdose = GI bleeding and acidosis; the chelator is deferoxamine.
also: Iron is one of few pills visible on x-ray
Free iron damages membranes by lipid peroxidation
Urine turns vin rose with deferoxamine
Deferasirox is an oral chelator for chronic iron overload

stem: A 36-year-old man and several co-workers are brought in together after spraying a field with pesticide. Each has drooling, tearing, pinpoint pupils, wheezing with copious bronchial secretions, and twitching of muscles.
oneliner: 36M + co-workers sprayed pesticide + salivation + miosis + bronchorrhea + fasciculations → treatment pair?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate pair of drugs?

whyNot.A: Physostigmine is itself a **cholinesterase inhibitor** and would worsen the picture
whyNot.B: Neostigmine **adds cholinesterase inhibition**; glycopyrrolate cannot offset that
whyNot.C: Naloxone and flumazenil reverse **opioids and benzodiazepines**, not secretions and miosis
whyNot.D: Dantrolene and cooling treat **hyperthermic syndromes**, not cholinergic excess

why: **Pesticide exposure** with **miosis, secretions, bronchorrhea and fasciculations** is cholinergic toxicity from **organophosphate** poisoning. **Atropine** blocks muscarinic effects and **pralidoxime** reactivates acetylcholinesterase.

idea.rule: Organophosphate poisoning needs an antimuscarinic for the signs and an oxime for the enzyme.
also: Atropine does not help nicotinic weakness
Pralidoxime works only before aging
Mnemonic DUMBELS: diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchospasm, emesis, lacrimation, salivation
Carbamates inhibit the enzyme reversibly

stem: A 52-year-old man with schizophrenia has been taking fluphenazine for 6 weeks. He now has a resting hand tremor, slow movements, a stiff face and a shuffling gait. He is not restless, strength is normal and there is no fever.
oneliner: 52M + fluphenazine for 6 weeks + tremor + bradykinesia + shuffling gait + not restless, no fever → treatment?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

whyNot.A: Levodopa is **unlikely to work** and may **worsen psychosis**; the D2 receptors are **blocked**, not the neurons lost
whyNot.B: Dantrolene is used for **neuroleptic malignant syndrome**, which needs **fever**; he is afebrile
whyNot.D: Propranolol helps **akathisia** (restlessness); he is **not restless** but slow
whyNot.E: Valbenazine (VMAT2 inhibitor) treats **tardive dyskinesia**, involuntary choreiform movements, not **slow, stiff movement**

answer: Benztropine (anticholinergic), or switch to a lower-potency or atypical agent
why: **Weeks of a typical antipsychotic** followed by **tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity** is **drug-induced parkinsonism** from D2 blockade. An **anticholinergic** such as **benztropine** restores the dopamine-acetylcholine balance.

idea.rule: Drug-induced parkinsonism: block of D2 leaves acetylcholine unopposed, so an anticholinergic helps.
also: Acute dystonia occurs within days and is treated with benztropine
Akathisia is treated with propranolol or benzodiazepines
Tardive dyskinesia is treated with VMAT2 inhibitors
Parkinsonism is more frequent with high-potency drugs

stem: A 37-year-old woman taking sertraline for depression added a tryptophan supplement 2 days ago. She is agitated and sweating, with diarrhea, a temperature of 38.9 C, tremor, inducible clonus in both ankles and brisk reflexes.
oneliner: 37F + sertraline + new tryptophan + agitation + diarrhea + fever + clonus and hyperreflexia → treatment?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

whyNot.B: Dantrolene is for **malignant hyperthermia** and NMS, which lack the **clonus and hyperreflexia** she has
whyNot.C: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist for **NMS**; it has serotonergic activity and can **worsen** this picture
whyNot.D: Physostigmine reverses **anticholinergic poisoning**, with dry skin; she is **sweating**
whyNot.E: Flumazenil reverses **benzodiazepines**, which she has not taken

answer: Stop the serotonergic drugs and give cyproheptadine
why: **Two serotonergic agents** with **clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, diarrhea and fever** make serotonin syndrome. Stop the drugs and give **cyproheptadine**, a **5-HT2A antagonist**.

idea.rule: Serotonin syndrome: stop the agents, then block 5-HT2A with cyproheptadine.
also: Neuromuscular findings (clonus) separate it from NMS
Onset is within hours, unlike NMS
MAOIs plus SSRIs, meperidine or linezolid can cause it
Benzodiazepines control agitation

stem: A 44-year-old woman who has taken alprazolam daily for years is found drowsy after an intentional overdose. Her blood pressure and heart rate are near normal, her breathing is shallow, and her pupils are normal. Flumazenil is being considered.
oneliner: 44F + years of alprazolam + sedated after overdose + near-normal vitals + shallow breathing → which statement about reversal is correct?
ask: Which of the following statements about reversal is most accurate?

options.A: Naloxone often causes seizures in dependent benzodiazepine users
options.B: Physostigmine is the safest antidote for this overdose
options.C: Flumazenil should be given routinely to every benzodiazepine overdose
options.D: Hemodialysis is the first-line treatment for benzodiazepine overdose
options.E: Flumazenil can precipitate seizures in a long-term user

whyNot.A: Naloxone reverses **opioids**, not benzodiazepines, and has **no relation to this dependence**
whyNot.B: Physostigmine treats **anticholinergic** poisoning and does not reverse GABA-A effects
whyNot.C: Flumazenil is **not routine**; it is avoided in **long-term users** like her, and **airway support** comes first
whyNot.D: Benzodiazepines are **highly protein-bound**, so dialysis helps little; **airway support** is first

answer: Flumazenil can cause withdrawal seizures in dependent patients
why: **Chronic benzodiazepine use** with sedation and **shallow breathing**: respiratory depression is the main danger, so support the **airway** first. **Flumazenil**, a **GABA-A benzodiazepine-site antagonist**, can **precipitate seizures** by triggering abrupt withdrawal, so it is usually avoided.

idea.rule: Reversing a drug the body depends on can cause withdrawal, here seizures.
also: Naloxone can precipitate acute opioid withdrawal in dependent users
Flumazenil is risky with co-ingested tricyclics or other proconvulsants
Benzodiazepine overdose alone is rarely fatal; supportive care is first
Flumazenil is short-acting, so sedation can return

stem: A 6-year-old boy living in an old house with peeling paint is hyperactive and has a microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling. He now has an unsteady gait, repeated vomiting and papilledema. Head CT shows cerebral edema.
oneliner: 6M + old house, peeling paint + microcytic anemia + basophilic stippling + ataxia + cerebral edema → which chelator?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate chelation therapy?

whyNot.A: Deferoxamine chelates **iron**, which is not the exposure here
whyNot.C: Oral succimer alone is for **milder lead poisoning**, not **encephalopathy with cerebral edema**
whyNot.E: Fomepizole blocks **alcohol dehydrogenase** for methanol and ethylene glycol

answer: Dimercaprol plus calcium EDTA (succimer if mild)
why: **Old paint**, **microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling** and **encephalopathy** indicate severe lead poisoning. **Encephalopathy or a very high level** calls for **dimercaprol plus calcium EDTA** (dimercaprol first); milder cases use **oral succimer**.

idea.rule: Severe lead toxicity with encephalopathy needs two parenteral chelators together.
also: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase
Lead lines appear at the gum margin and long-bone metaphyses
Wrist and foot drop occur in adults
Succimer is oral and used in mild disease

stem: A physician notices raised liver enzymes in several patients taking a drug that was approved and marketed 4 months ago. No published reports exist yet about this effect. The drug is still prescribed widely.
oneliner: Physician + newly marketed drug already on sale + raised liver enzymes in several patients + no published data → what action applies?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Begin a new phase 1 study in healthy volunteers
options.B: Begin a new phase 2 study in treated patients
options.C: Stop it in affected patients and file a MedWatch report
options.D: Begin a new phase 3 randomized trial of the drug
options.E: Stop the drug in all patients and take no action

whyNot.A: Phase 1 studies are **pre-approval safety trials** in few volunteers
whyNot.B: Phase 2 studies are **pre-approval** dose and efficacy tests
whyNot.D: Phase 3 trials are **pre-approval** confirmatory trials of efficacy
whyNot.E: Stopping the drug in everyone and **not reporting** leaves other patients exposed

answer: Report to FDA MedWatch (phase 4 postmarketing surveillance)
why: A drug **already marketed** with new adverse effects is in **phase 4 postmarketing surveillance**. The physician should **stop it in affected patients** and report the reaction to **FDA MedWatch**.

idea.rule: After approval, rare adverse effects are caught by voluntary reports in phase 4.
also: Phase 1: safety in healthy volunteers
Phase 2: efficacy and dose in patients
Phase 3: large trial versus standard care
Phase 4 can lead to a drug being withdrawn
